question: How can a piece built on one continuous ripple still build, break and return?
intro: The longest of the five pieces: the left hand ripples almost without a break while slow notes float above it, and two great swells of sound rise and fall. Same Lviv performance as the rest of Miroirs.

sections.label: A · The barque in F♯ minor
B · The swell and the sweeping runs
B′ · The sweeping runs return in E♭
sections.mNote: fortissimo sweeping runs return in a new key region

sections.label: D · F♯ minor, a high repeated figure
A′ · The opening figure returns
sections.mNote: opening ripple returns very quietly and closes the piece

cues.title: A boat, wrapped in pedal
cues.text: Marked D’un rythme souple, très enveloppé de pédales: a supple rhythm, wrapped in pedal. In F♯ minor, rippling figures in the left hand run almost without a break beneath slow, tied notes in the right. At nearly seven minutes in this recording, it is the longest of the five pieces.
cues.evidence: The marking and the texture are on scan p. 14 of the first edition (IMSLP #02693); the key is on IMSLP’s work page. The report shows steady activity (2.6–3.2 attacks a second) and the pitch classes C♯, F♯, A through the first 20 seconds. The five Commons files run 3:34–6:43; this is the longest.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A dozen seconds in 3/4
cues.text: Around 0:25 the texture changes: the left hand moves into a wider bass-clef arpeggio in 3/4 for about a dozen seconds, and the recording’s key estimate leans towards A major. By 0:40 the opening ripple has returned.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundaries at 0:26 (0.61) and 0:38 (0.66) bracket this stretch. Its key estimate there is A major (0.79–0.86 at 0:25–0:35) and then C♯ minor (0.80–0.81 at 0:40–0:45); these are chroma-based guesses, not a score analysis, and the score’s written key signature (scan pp. 14–15, IMSLP #02693) stays that of F♯ minor/A major. The 3/4 signature is at the foot of scan p. 14 and the opening signature returns on scan p. 15.

cues.title: For a painter of the Apaches
cues.text: Ravel dedicated this piece to Paul Sordes, a painter in the Apaches. The group met on Saturdays, often in his studio, and members announced themselves at the door by whistling the opening of Borodin’s Second Symphony, which Ravel had suggested as their theme.
cues.evidence: The dedication is on IMSLP’s work page. The Saturday meetings, the Sordes studio and the Borodin theme are in Wikipedia’s article on Les Apaches (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Apaches).

cues.title: A short bar, then the swell
cues.text: At 1:12 a short bar marked sforzando opens a long crescendo, from pp en dehors: chromatic runs rise and fall in the right hand over bass notes. The level climbs to its peak at about 1:25, the loudest 5-second window of the whole recording.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 1:12 (0.78); the level rises from −15.0 dB at 1:10 to −8.2 dB at 1:20 and −4.8 dB at 1:25, which is the loudest window in the report. The sf bar, the pp en dehors and the crescendo are on scan p. 17.

cues.title: Runs sweep both hands
cues.text: From 1:40 fortissimo runs sweep across the keyboard, with the right hand an octave higher. Each is marked diminuendo and followed by a quiet bar of chords. The report counts four to seven attacks a second in these bars.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 1:40 (0.51) and onset rates of 5.8 a second at 1:40, 3.8–4.0 at 1:45–1:50 and 6.6 at 1:55, against about 2 before. The ff and fff sweeps, the diminuendo and the quiet chord bars are on scan pp. 18–19.

cues.title: Très expressif
cues.text: Around 2:00 the sweeping runs give way to a rising right-hand glissando and then a lyrical phrase marked très expressif, with melody above slow bass arpeggios. The level stays steady and the attack rate settles at about two a second.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 2:00 (0.42); the onset rate falls from 3.0 at 2:00 to 1.8–2.2 a second by 2:15 and the level holds between −8 and −12 dB. The glissando and the très expressif marking are on scan p. 19; the start of the phrase is estimated.

cues.title: A line from Julius Caesar
cues.text: Ravel explained the title Miroirs with a line from Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: the eye sees not itself but by reflection. In his 1928 sketch he said it did not mean a subjective theory of art, and he accepted the label impressionist only by analogy.
cues.evidence: The Shakespeare line is in Kyle Fyr, “Mapping Ravel’s ‘La vallée des cloches’”, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 5 (https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html), citing Orenstein. The remarks on subjectivism and impressionism are quoted from the 1928 Esquisse autobiographique at https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miroirs_(Ravel).

cues.title: Three flats and the runs return
cues.text: At 3:04 a double bar brings three flats and an E♭ region. The recording jumps from about −16 dB to −9.5 dB, and the fortissimo sweeping runs of the first half come back, again followed by quiet chords.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundary at 3:04 scores 0.98; the level rises from −15.9 dB at 3:00 to −9.5 dB at 3:05 and the onset rate to 4.2–4.8 a second, with a key estimate near B♭ major (a chroma-based guess). The three-flat signature and the ff sweeps are on scan pp. 21–22, and the PTNA Piano Encyclopedia analysis reads this return as the second B section.

cues.title: F♯ minor returns
cues.text: At 3:38, the strongest change in the recording, three sharps replace three flats and F♯ minor returns. Shortly afterwards a quick high figure starts in the right hand, marked pp sans nuances (without shading), while the left hand sings a slow line.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundary at 3:38 scores 1.00; its key estimate moves to F♯ minor (0.76–0.85), the onset rate to 5.0–5.6 a second and the brightness to 1131–1245 Hz at 3:45–3:55, while the 3:50 window is the quietest in the middle of the piece (−22.9 dB). The three-sharp signature is at the foot of scan p. 22; the pp sans nuances figure is on scan p. 23.

cues.title: Ravel scored it himself
cues.text: Ravel orchestrated this piece in 1906 and revised the orchestration in 1926. Alborada del gracioso, which he scored more than a decade later, is the only other piece of Miroirs he orchestrated.
cues.evidence: IMSLP’s work page for Miroirs states that Ravel orchestrated Nos. 3 and 4, No. 3 in 1906 (revised in 1926) and No. 4 in 1918; Wikipedia’s Alborada del gracioso article dates the orchestral premiere to 17 May 1919, so the exact year of No. 4 is left open here.

cues.title: Augmentez peu à peu
cues.text: Marked augmentez, peu à peu — increase, little by little — the chords under the repeated figure grow denser from about 4:40. The level climbs by roughly 14 dB in 25 seconds.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 4:42 (0.62); the level rises from −20.6 dB at 4:35 to −6.1 dB at 5:00. The aug-men-tez and peu a peu markings are on scan pp. 25–26.

cues.title: The second summit
cues.text: At about 4:55–5:10 fortissimo chords and sweeping runs, marked ff and fff, reach the peak of the second half. Four of the report’s five loudest windows are in this stretch.
cues.evidence: The loudest windows in the report are 1:25, 5:00, 5:05, 4:55 and 5:10, so four of the five fall in 4:55–5:10. The ff and fff markings and the sweeping runs are on scan p. 26.

cues.title: Seven weeks on a yacht
cues.text: In June and July 1905 Ravel went on a seven-week Rhine cruise aboard the yacht of Alfred Edwards, owner of Le Matin, and his wife Misia. It was his first trip abroad. Neither cited account links the cruise to this piece, which he had finished by the end of that year.
cues.evidence: The cruise is in Wikipedia’s Maurice Ravel article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel). That Miroirs was complete six months after June 1905 is in Kyle Fyr, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 3. Neither account connects the cruise to Une barque.

cues.title: Le trémolo très fondu
cues.text: From about 5:25 low figures repeat above a rolling accompaniment, and later in the passage Ravel marks le trémolo très fondu, a tremolo that must melt into its surroundings. Compare the quiet attack rate here with the sweeping runs of the summit.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 5:26 (0.71) and an onset rate of 1.4–1.6 a second at 5:30–5:35, after 4.0 at 5:25. The tremolo marking is on scan p. 27 (system 3); its exact bar is not aligned with the recording.

cues.title: The opening ripple returns
cues.text: At 6:18 the opening figure comes back. The report’s strongest pitch classes (C♯, F♯, A) and its C♯ minor label are the same as at 0:00. The ripple is quiet and shorter than at the start.
cues.evidence: The report’s boundary at 6:18 scores 0.72; from 6:20 the local key is C♯ minor (0.77–0.86) in the pitch classes C♯, F♯, A, as at 0:00–0:20 (C♯ minor, 0.82–0.84). The return of the opening texture is on scan p. 30, and the PTNA Piano Encyclopedia analysis closes the form with the opening motif.

cues.title: A chord marked pppp
cues.text: The score ends on a rolled chord marked pppp. In this recording the level falls from −25 dB at 6:35 to −38.6 dB at 6:40, the two quietest windows of the whole file.
cues.evidence: The quietest 5-second windows in the report are 6:40 and 6:35 (−38.6 and −25.1 dB); the file ends at 6:43. The rolled final chord and the pppp are on the last bar of scan p. 30.

transitions.title: The ripple sinks into the bass
transitions.how: The opening ripple is left behind. A new passage in 3/4, marked p, puts a wide arpeggio in the bass clef under short right-hand phrases. Then 2/4 bars follow in which the right hand falls almost silent and the left hand sinks towards the bottom of the keyboard. Ravel keeps the pedal and the continuous left-hand motion but removes the singing right-hand line that gave the opening its shape.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundary at 0:56 scores 0.90 and the detected attack rate falls to 0.6–1.0 a second at 1:05–1:10; its key estimates (D and G major, 0.72–0.86, at 0:55–1:10) are chroma-based guesses, not a score analysis. The 3/4 and 2/4 bars are on scan p. 16 of the first edition (IMSLP #02693); exact bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: A sforzando starts the long crescendo
transitions.how: The quiet 2/4 bars end at a double bar. A one-beat bar marked sforzando, with low bass notes under a silent right hand, breaks the stillness. Another double bar brings 3/4, now pp en dehors (bring it out), with rolled chords and low octaves in the left hand and chromatic runs in the right that rise and fall and cre–scen–do. The left-hand motion that carried the first half becomes the base of an increase in sound that peaks at fortissimo.
transitions.evidence: The report has a boundary at 1:12 (0.78) and the level rises from −15.0 dB at 1:10 to −4.8 dB at 1:25, the loudest window of the recording. The sf bar, the 3/4 pp en dehors passage and the cre–scen–do are on scan pp. 16–17 of the first edition.

transitions.title: A glissando leads to a singing line
transitions.how: After the last fortissimo sweep, marked diminuendo, the music falls to mezzo-forte. A right-hand glissando rises over low bass octaves, and the writing settles into 2/4 with a melody in the right hand marked très expressif above slow bass arpeggios. The runs of the previous page disappear and a lyrical line takes their place.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundary at 2:00 scores 0.42; the onset rate falls from 5.8 at 1:40 and 6.6 at 1:55 to 3.0 at 2:00 and 1.8–2.2 by 2:15. The diminuendo, the glissando and the très expressif bars are on scan p. 19. The exact bar is not aligned.

transitions.title: A double bar brings three flats
transitions.how: The quiet, repeating 2/4 bars end at a double bar. The key signature changes to three flats and the music moves to an E♭ region in 3/4, pp, with a fast right-hand figure an octave higher. Within a few bars the dynamic jumps to fortissimo, with a crescendo in the left hand, and the same sweeping runs of the first half return. There is no cadence between the keys: the double bar makes the change.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundary at 3:04 scores 0.98; the level rises from −15.9 dB at 3:00 to −9.5 dB at 3:05 and the onset rate to 4.2–4.8 a second. The double bar, three-flat signature and ff sweeps are on scan p. 21 (systems 2–4) of the first edition.

transitions.title: Back to three sharps, quietly
transitions.how: The sweeping runs end on a short, quiet phrase marked mp très expressif, and a double bar replaces the three flats with three sharps. F♯ minor returns. After a few bars marked sf and p, the right hand settles on a quick high figure, pp sans nuances (without shading), that repeats for many bars while the left hand carries a slow line marked p expressif. The restless runs give way to a steady, shimmering figure.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundary at 3:38 scores 1.00, the strongest in the recording; its key estimate moves to F♯ minor and the onset rate to 5.0–5.6 a second at 3:45–3:55, with the level falling to −22.9 dB at 3:50. The mp très expressif bars and the new key signature are at the foot of scan p. 22; the pp sans nuances figure is on scan p. 23.

transitions.title: After the summit, a tremolo and a hush
transitions.how: After the ff and fff sweeps the dynamic falls away: in this recording the detected attack rate drops to 0.4 a second at 5:20. Repeated figures then sit above a rolling accompaniment, and Ravel writes le trémolo très fondu, a tremolo that must melt into its surroundings. The page after it continues quieter still, at pp and ppp in 3/4, with rising and falling figures in the right hand. The long climb is answered by a hush and a softer texture.
transitions.evidence: The level falls from −7.9 dB at 5:10 to −16.7 dB at 5:20 and the onset rate to 0.4 a second; the report’s boundary at 5:26 scores 0.71. The tremolo marking is on scan p. 27 (system 3) and the pp and ppp continuation in 3/4 on scan p. 28. Exact bars are not aligned with the recording.

transitions.title: Low chords, then the ripple returns
transitions.how: The paired time signatures, 2/4 and 6/8, were restored at the foot of scan p. 28 and stay in force. The quiet continuation gives way on pp. 29–30 to low repeated chords in the left hand with accented chords above, marked mf and falling away. At pp the left-hand ripple in F♯ minor then returns, and the right hand’s tied notes lie above it as at the start. It is the opening figure again, much quieter; the reprise lasts about 25 seconds against the opening’s 56.
transitions.evidence: The report’s boundary at 6:18 scores 0.72; the level falls from −10.2 dB at 6:00 to −20.2 dB at 6:15, and from 6:20 its key estimate is C♯ minor (0.77–0.86) in the opening’s pitch classes C♯, F♯ and A, as at 0:00–0:20. The paired signatures first appear at the foot of scan p. 28, the low mf chords run from p. 29 into p. 30, and the returning ripple is on scan p. 30 of the first edition. The exact bar is not aligned.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; composition with Fauré from 1897, counterpoint with André Gedalge
Les Apaches: Ricardo Viñes, Maurice Delage, Tristan Klingsor, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi and other musicians, writers and painters
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum preserving his piano and collections
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber music and piano works; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
